query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In equimolar solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles, the onset of premelting is governed by the local segregation and enhanced atomic mobility of the lowest-melting-point element (copper). As the particle is gradually heated in an inert atmosphere, copper atoms preferentially migrate toward surfaces and grain boundaries, producing local regions with reduced effective melting temperatures that nucleate a premelted (liquid-like) phase before the overall nanoparticle undergoes full melting.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogeneous, solid equimolar iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles synthesized to have a uniform single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Gradual heating of the nanoparticles in a controlled inert atmosphere across the premelting regime into the melting regime while monitoring structural and compositional changes in situ.
generation.conditions: Inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation, a slow and controlled heating rate to accurately resolve temperature-dependent local transformations, and a measurement setup (e.g., in situ TEM with EDX or synchrotron XRD) capable of detecting nanoscale elemental segregation and phase change.
generation.structural_mediator: Local enrichment of copper at surfaces and grain boundaries leading to heterogeneously reduced melting points within the nanoparticles.
generation.mechanism: Due to its significantly lower melting point relative to Fe, Ni, Cr, and Co, copper atoms have a higher mobility at elevated temperatures. This mobility drives a nanoscale segregation process during heating, where copper accumulates in localized regions. These copper-rich areas effectively lower the local melting point, initiating a premelting phase that then propagates and facilitates the complete melting of the nanoparticle.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline nanoparticle that maintains uniform elemental distribution, the nanoparticles undergoing copper segregation will exhibit early signs of premelting (such as surface fluidity, local loss of crystalline order, or formation of liquid-like regions) at temperatures below the bulk average melting point of the alloy. These features should be detectable as local composition gradients and structural changes prior to global melting.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles that retain a uniform, single-phase solid solution without significant elemental segregation, showing a melting behavior consistent with the averaged bulk melting characteristics.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles formed as homogeneous equimolar solid solutions and heated in inert environments. It is most relevant when the alloy contains at least one significantly lower-melting-point element (here, copper) and for particle sizes where surface and grain boundary effects are prominent.
generation.uncertainty: The degree and spatial extent of copper segregation and its precise impact on the local melting temperature are not fully quantified. Temperature ranges for onset of segregation versus complete premelting may vary with particle size and synthesis history.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ heating experiments on equimolar iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper nanoparticles in an inert atmosphere using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) to spatially resolve elemental distributions and phase transitions in real time. A controlled heating ramp should be applied to traverse the premelting regime.
measurements: Spatially resolved elemental maps (focusing on copper distribution) at incremental temperature steps.
Real-time TEM imaging to detect onset of local disorder or liquid-like regions.
Temperature-dependent diffraction patterns to monitor loss of crystallinity in copper-rich areas.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, upon gradual heating, the nanoparticles do not show any detectable local enrichment of copper (or any preferential segregation of a low-melting component) before the onset of uniform melting, and if the premelting behavior occurs uniformly at the bulk melting temperature without localized early transformation, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The phase formation mechanism of HEAPs is mainly related to the alloying behavior of components during mechanical alloying. Due to the small difference in physical properties and electronegativity of elements in the CoCrCuFeMnNix HEA system, the alloying process is mainly diffusion-controlled. The diffusion rates of alloying elements are different due to their physical properties. Chen et al. [] showed that elements with a low melting point or brittle crystal structure may be preferentially dissolved during ball milling. Figure 9 shows the melting point and thermal conductivity of each element in the CoCrCuFeMnNi HEA system []. The melting points of Co and Ni are very similar, but Ni with an FCC phase has higher plasticity than Co with an HCP phase, so the alloying of Co occurs before Ni. Therefore, the alloying sequence of CoCrCuFeMnNix HEAPs during ball milling is Cu→Mn→Co→Ni→Fe→Cr. cited_evidence.text: Microstructural stability is one of the most important factors for alloys to be used at elevated temperatures. A stable alloy can maintain its properties without substantial changes, even after extended periods of service (). The minor presence of impurity interstitials, e.g., nitrogen and oxygen, in the equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy studied was found to introduce uncertainties in its mechanical properties at the aging temperature by facilitating phase segregation at the nanoscale and reducing the solid strengthening effect. Furthermore, the depletion of impurity interstitials in regions adjacent to grain boundaries leads to the formation of PFZs. This spatially confined compositional variation nearby grain boundaries creates very high local electrochemical and mechanical contrast, often affecting the alloy’s corrosion and mechanical properties (). To improve the stability of RHEAs for high-temperature applications, the impurities must be better controlled.
